rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Hydrogen sulphide is the qualitative analyst's scalpel. Made on demand in **Kipp's apparatus** (FeS + dil. H₂SO₄ → FeSO₄ + H₂S; three bulbs, pressure-valve self-stopping) and dried over **P₂O₅**, it is a colourless rotten-egg gas — dangerously poisonous and able to numb its own smell. In water it is a **weak dibasic acid** (NaHS, Na₂S).…

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "Hydrogen sulphide is a weak dibasic acid and a strong reducing agent; it precipitates metal sulphides selectively according to the acidity of the solution."

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***The yellow snowfall*** - every reduction H2S performs ends the same way: fine yellow sulphur raining out of solution - the visible signature of S2- climbing to S0.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — The Stinking Gas That Analyses Metals H₂S: prepared from Kipp's apparatus, acidic in water, a classical analytical reagent (metal sulphide precipitation in groups), and a reducing agent. Preparation, properties, analytical role, uses.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 Preparation — Kipp's apparatus - **FeS + dil. H₂SO₄ → FeSO₄ + H₂S↑** (in the middle globe of Kipp's apparatus; iron sulphide lumps in the middle bulb, acid in the top reservoir). - **Kipp's apparatus:** three-bulb glass device — acid in the top bulb flows down to the middle bulb containing FeS lumps; gas evolves; when the stopcock is closed, gas pressure pushes acid back up into…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Kipp's: 3 bulbs, pressure valve logic. Dry over P2O5. Group II in acid (CuS, CdS); Group IV in alkali (ZnS, MnS). Reducer: Fe3+ -> Fe2+, I2 -> I-, MnO4- -> Mn2+, all giving yellow S. Limited air burns to S, excess to SO2.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: The pH knob runs qualitative analysis: acidity suppresses H2S ionisation so only ultra-insoluble Group II sulphides fall out, while alkalinity multiplies S2- and drags Group IV down too - one reagent, two regimes, controlled selectivity.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: H2S prep: FeS + dil H2SO4 -> FeSO4 + H2S in KIPP'S APPARATUS (3 bulbs: acid reservoir top, FeS middle, gas collects bottom; closing stopcock pushes acid back up - self-regulating). Pure/dry: Sb2S3 + 6HCl -> 2SbCl3 + 3H2S; dry over P2O5 (NOT conc H2SO4 - oxidises H2S).…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: H2S can be more dangerous than HCN at comparable exposures because it anaesthetises the sense of smell - victims stop noticing the warning.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: **NEB-style (2m): How does H2S act as an analytical reagent in qualitative analysis?** — H₂S supplies S²⁻ ions whose concentration is controlled by acidity. In **acidic medium** the ionisation of H₂S is suppressed, so only the **extremely insoluble Group II sulphides** precipitate: **CuS** (black),…

rows.text: ## 3. Scientific Definitions | Term | Scientific meaning | Example | |---|---|---| | **Kipp's apparatus** | Self-regulating gas generator | FeS + dil. H₂SO₄ → H₂S | | **Dibasic acid** | Two replaceable H per molecule | H₂S → NaHS, Na₂S | | **Group II sulphides** | Sulphides precipitated in acid medium by H₂S | CuS, CdS | | **Group IV sulphides** | Sulphides needing alkaline…  ·  ## 4. Detailed Explanation ### 4.1 Why Kipp's apparatus is clever - Gas pressure does the valving: open stopcock → acid falls to FeS → gas flows; close stopcock → pressure lifts acid out of contact → reaction stops. No taps of reagents, no heating — a 19th-century design still in every qualitative-analysis lab.…  ·  ## 5. Comparison Tables | Medium | [S²⁻] | Sulphides precipitated | Examples | |---|---|---|---| | acidic (HCl) | very low | Group II only | CuS, CdS, HgS, As₂S₃ | | alkaline (NH₄OH) | high | Group II + IV | ZnS, MnS, NiS, CoS, FeS |

H₂SO₄ oxidises H₂S to sulphur; use **P₂O₅**. - **"H₂S is a strong acid because S is big."** It is a **weak** dibasic acid — the S–H bond is strong and H₂S is poorly ionised; acidity is not size alone.…  ·  ## 7.
